column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The article gives estimates of 60,000-250,000 for the population; kept as a range.

The entry says Nguyen Kim restored a Le emperor in Thanh Hoa in 1533; the article has him proclaiming Prince Le Ninh king in 1533 while based in Laos (Xam Neua). The place of the proclamation is left out.

The article says he became a lawyer in 1518 and was called to the Parlement of Dole 'at the age of 34', which does not fit a birth in 1486; the year and age are left out. The article says he was appointed chancellor of the empire soon after 1519; the entry calls him keeper of the seals from the 1530s. The title is left out.

The entry says she was later merged with Gula; the article describes partial conflation after the end of the third millennium BCE and warns against full identification. The text says only that scholars warn against treating them as interchangeable, which does not contradict the entry. The dog burials at her temple are in the entry, not in this excerpt of the article; not repeated.

The article reports that some scholars place Kalinga and Sinhapura in Sumatra or on the Jaffna Peninsula, and that Indian historians do not find his parents' names; the entry calls him a prince from Kalinga in eastern India. The location debate is left out. The article does not tell his death, so the last section is not 'Death and legacy'.

The article is thin and mostly lists (bands, notable people). It also lists Lytton Indian Band under the Nlaka'pamux Nation Tribal Council while saying the Lytton First Nation belongs to no tribal association; the council membership of Lytton is left out. The article's statement that no Nlaka'pamux government is in the treaty process 'at present' is left out as a present-day status.
The entry dates Muhammad Nurbakhsh 1393-1464; the article gives his death as 1465. Neither date is printed.

The article gives the sequence twice in different orders (wheat, turnips, barley, clover or ryegrass; and wheat, turnips, clover and barley); the order is not repeated in the text. The article calls clover and ryegrass legumes; ryegrass is a grass, so only clover is named as a legume.

The entry says the Kokura branch ruled until 1871; the article says 1632 through 1868. No end year is printed. The entry says the clan took its name from an estate in Kai province; the article places its origin in Shinano and does not mention Kai. Left out. The article's lead gives the Sengoku period as c. 1185-1600, which is wrong; not used.
The 2006 proposal for Virginia's interim state song and the lists of top songs (Western Writers of America, CBS News 2026) are left out as rankings or minor detail.

The entry says Tolteca-Chichimeca groups drove them from Cholula in the 12th century; the article gives the Chichimec conquest as the year 1 Flint, which may be 1168, 1240 or 1292. The date of the conquest is left out.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 250 words in all, mostly film appearances, and its lyrics section is empty

The article's statement that the lake was 'one of the most polluted lakes in the United States' is left out as a ranking. The 1656 date of the Jesuit mission is in the entry; the article does not give it.

The entry calls him a god of war and fertility; the article calls him god of war and, in peace, of the fine arts. 'Fertility' is not repeated and not contradicted. The decline after Christian conversion in the 1810s is in the entry, not in the article.

The article calls Mudrarakshasa a Buddhist drama; the word is left out as doubtful. The identification with the Parthians and the Pallava theory are in the entry; the article excerpt does not discuss the Pallavas.

The article says the Panchganga is formed by four streams, with an underground Saraswati added by local tradition; the entry says five streams. The text gives the four and the tradition of the fifth, which matches the name and does not contradict the entry. The Maratha states of Kolhapur are in the entry; the article has no history section.
The article dates U Seinda's Arakan rebellion both to May 1947 and to 1946; left out. The article spells the Chin leader both Vamthu Mawng and Vumthu Mawng; he is not named.

The entry says he governed the County of Urgell for his grandson; the article says he transferred the guardianship of his grandson Ermengol VI to Raymond Berengar III of Barcelona, and that he was in exile in Urgell 1103-1108. The guardianship is left out. The entry calls him a Leonese count, the article a Castilian nobleman; neither label is used.

The article gives two accounts of the renaming as Supreme Soviet of the Lithuanian SSR: on 25 August with the new constitution (lead), and right after the Soviet approval of 3 August as a provisional Supreme Soviet (Annexation section). No date of the renaming is printed.

The article contradicts itself on whether zamindars became owners (granted proprietorial rights) or remained revenue agents of the state; the text says only that their tenure was secured, which matches the entry's 'treated as landowners'. The present-day claims about Pakistan and Kenya are left out.

The article dates his elected terms 1978-1985 and 1989-1993; the entry's 'first elected governor in 1977' refers to the election, so the text speaks of elections only. Left out the 'as of May 2025' remark about Pula Nikolao Pula.
Article: established 'around 1200' / 'before 1200'; entry says late 12th century, consistent. Article calls Ivan III 'Tsar'; left out.

The article's lead says he returned to office in 1764; its body gives 1 January 1765 (and the lead's own range 1765-1775). Used the body's date. Article also says Alexander I pardoned him at the claimed age of 110; left out, since the birth year is disputed.
The article's Simon de Montfort 'brother-in-law' (Earl of Leicester, governor of Guyenne) is the younger Simon; kept the article's titles. Article spells Guy 'de Monfort' once; used Montfort.
The entry credits Basedow with Prince Leopold III Friedrich Franz's support; the article names Wolke as co-founder and calls the prince 'Prince Franz'.

SKIPPED: The article attributes the temple to Jayavarman VII as a Mahayana Buddhist foundation of the early 13th century, which contradicts the entry's 'probably as a Hindu shrine, later converted to Buddhist use'; without the origin, too little remains (about 200 words on the prayer hall, the banknote and the monkeys). Article: built by Jayavarman VII in the early 13th century, statue to Jayabuddhamahanatha, towers to Prajnaparamita, the Buddha and Avalokiteshvara; originally Mahayana, later Theravada under Ayutthaya. Entry: late 12th or early 13th century, probably Hindu, later Buddhist. The entry may need correcting.

Heading 'Discovery and study' is from the object list; the site is a place, but the excavation history is the main matter. The article puts the first village before Phylakopi I (2300 BCE); the entry dates occupation from about 2300 BCE, so no earlier date is given.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance. Article: born 11 March 1436; after his death he was briefly succeeded by his son Sinibaldo before Girolamo Riario acquired Forlì. The entry says Riario's grant on his death ended Ordelaffi rule, which passes over Sinibaldo.

Left out the article's unsourced claim that U-234's uranium oxide went into the Hiroshima bomb. The entry's 'fishing settlements from 1623' is not in the article; the article dates the first sawmill to 1623.
Article: died 2 August 914 or 923. Entry: d. 923 and archbishop to 923. The year of death is left out. Article spells the predecessor both 'Ethelred' and 'Æthelred'.
Left out the article's unexplained sentence about a tribe declining rice. The section on the pochteca after the conquest is empty in the article.

The article says Indians were later added as a separate classification, while the entry calls them a subgroup; the text leaves the point out. The Dickson school's town is spelt 'Plettenburg Bay' in the article; left out.

The article is muddled on dedication: one section calls the c. 510 BCE three-cell temple the sanctuary of Minerva, another the temple of Apollo with Minerva's cult in a separate older nucleus. The entry calls it Minerva's; the text describes the temple without naming its god. The article also dates the sanctuary complex to the 7th century BC in one place and the first buildings to about 530 BC in another; both left out. Vulca is not named in the article.

The article says a silted lagoon behind Calais now seems the most likely area; the entry says most scholars identify the port with Boulogne. The text gives the arguments without saying which view prevails. The 30 Roman miles of the entry are not in the article.
The article gives the Association in the East as established in 1944 in one place and 1947 in another; the date is left out. Left out the article's projection that the church may be extinct by 2033.

Entry: the colony was sold to the Dutch in 1717. Article: the sale became known in 1717, John Canoe resisted about seven years and the Dutch took the fort in 1724; it also dates the colony 1682-1721. The text says only that the intention to sell was learned by 1717. Entry names the Brandenburg African Company, which the article does not.

SKIPPED: The article contradicts the entry on his parentage and on how he gained Scinawa, which is most of what it tells; a longer text could not avoid contradicting the entry. Article: Przemko was the youngest son of Konrad I, Duke of Glogow, and Salome of Greater Poland; Henry III of Glogow was his older brother and guardian. He received Zagan in 1278 and took Scinawa in 1284 by exchange with his brother Konrad II the Hunchback, under pressure from Henry IV Probus. Born 1255/65; died 26 February 1289 at Siewierz (Dlugosz gives 1290). The entry says he was a son of Henry III and received Scinawa as his share of his father's lands: the entry looks wrong and needs a second source.
The article's lead says the agency dealt with forty princely states; its 1941 Census list gives 16 plus 18. The text cites only the census.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance, and it gives some two thousand inscriptions where the entry says several hundred. Article: attested 500 BCE to 200 CE, some two thousand inscriptions in the Musnad script, mainly in Wadi Bayhan and Wadi Harib; inscriptions end after Saba and Hadramawt defeated Qataban at the end of the 2nd century CE; Awsanian virtually identical. Entry: several hundred inscriptions.

The article gives his death as 1220 or 1221: most historians named (Abu Shamah, al-Dhahabi, Ibn Kathir, Sibt Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Mundhiri) date it to 617 AH (1220), Ibn al-Athir to 618 AH (1221). The entry has d. 1220; no death year is printed. The article dates his selection to 1200-01; the entry says he took Mecca in 1201. No year is printed for it. His age at death is given as about 70 (Ibn al-Athir) or about 90 (others); left out.

The article dates the agreement to spring 893; the entry says it was agreed in 892. No year is printed for it. The article says the caliph married her by proxy while she was in Egypt; the entry says the marriage was celebrated in Baghdad. Both the proxy marriage and her lavish arrival in Baghdad are printed, without saying where the celebration took place. The entry's claim that the trousseau helped exhaust the Tulunid treasury is not in the article; not repeated.

The article gives his death as 1538 at Ramiriquí; the entry has d. c. 1539. No death year is printed. The entry says he died in captivity; the article says he was deported to Suesca and then fled to Ramiriquí, where he died. The text says only that he was sent to Suesca and died shortly afterwards at Ramiriquí. The article calls his successor his nephew Quiminza; the entry and the article's last paragraph name Aquiminzaque. Only the statue's naming of Aquiminzaque is printed.

The entry dates the Shrinathji image's installation at Nathdwara to 1672; the article gives no year. None printed. The article's lead claims he 'defeated the Mughals' in the Rajput war and 'annexed many Mughal territories'; these claims are weakly supported in its body and were not printed beyond the specific raids it describes.

The article says the House of Ganesha ruled Bengal from 1415 to 1435; the entry says he seized power around 1414. No year of his seizure of power is printed. The article's statement that 'many independent sources confirm that Ibrahim Shah was thoroughly defeated' sits beside a Chinese source saying the invader was bought off with gold; only the attributed traditions are printed. The Dinajpur Raj's later zamindars in the article belong to the estate, not to Ganesha; left out.

The article dates his death to March 1592 and his reign to 1581-1592; the entry has d. 1593 and a reign of 1581 to 1593. No death year is printed. The article's lead says he received the name Rajasinha after the Battle of Mulleriyawa, its body (citing the Alakeshwara War and Rajavaliya) after the battle at Alutnuwara against Veediya Bandara. The text says only 'after one of these early victories'. The article dates the Battle of Mulleriyawa to 1562 but notes that de Menezes's term as captain-major (1559-1560) puts it after May 1559. No year is printed. The entry mentions the siege of Colombo in 1587-1588; the article names sieges of 1581 and 1587. Both years printed as the article gives them; check against the entry's 1587-1588.

The article dates the Battle of Koppam both to 1052 and to 1053-54; the entry gives 1054. No year is printed. The article dates his reign to 1052-1063 and gives him dates of 997-1063; the entry has r. c. 1052-1064. No end year is printed. The article also calls him the fifth of nine children; only the copper plate's 'third son' is printed, attributed to the plate.

The article's lead says he reigned until his death in 1279; its later section says only that he lived in obscurity at Pazhayarai until 1279, after which no Chola inscriptions are found. The text follows the entry's wording that he disappears from the record. The article's section 'Fate of Cholas' (Pandya retribution, Pichavaram chiefs, Nagama Nayak) is unsourced and confused; left out.

The article says he was leader of the opposition after the 1957 election and also finance minister 'in this government' without naming the coalition; the text keeps the order the article gives without dating his entry into the government. The article says Patna merged with the Union of India in 1948; the entry says it merged into Orissa. The text says only 'his state's merger'. The article's spelling 'St. Columbia's College' is printed as St. Columba's College, the usual spelling; the check may flag it. His grandson's present office is left out (a present-day position).

The article dates Malik Kafur's campaign 'around 1308' in its lead and '1308' in the body; the entry says 1308. Consistent; no year needed in the text beyond what is printed. Isami's claim that the daughter was the mother of Shihab-ud-din Omar, and Firishta's that Malik Kafur married her, are left out.

The article is short and rests largely on his official biography; the text attributes the passports claim to it. The article says only that Humaid is his son and the current ruler; that Humaid followed him directly is inferred from Humaid being named crown prince in 1960.
The article's 2001 literacy figures and the forecast that they 'should improve' are left out. The entry mentions spring festivals around Holi; the article does not, so nothing is added on them.

The article calls him a nobleman from Lombardy; the entry says Verona. Neither is printed. The article says he agreed to marry Isabella sometime before 25 May 1212, the day the dispensation was received; the text follows that reading.

The entry says the war ended soon after his death; the article says only that it 'petered out' after 1418. The text keeps to the last campaigns of his reign. The article's lead calls him one of the most famous kings in Burmese history; left out as praise.
Article years are given as BC; printed as BCE. The entry's c. 1040 BCE matches the article's rising in 1042 BCE and three years of war.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the entry (epithets, the Baratella finds, the identification with Artemis and Diana)

The article gives inconsistent figures for the women added (8.4, 8.5 and 9.2 million) and the men added (5.2 and 4.5 million); none is printed, only the totals of 7.7 and 21.4 million. The article says the electorate 'tripled'; the entry says 'nearly tripled'. The text gives the figures without either word.

The article gives the rebel force as 10,000 to 20,000; the entry says some 20,000. No figure is printed. The article does not name Zipaquirá or the Capitulations and gives no year for Galán's execution; the entry's 1782 is not repeated.

The entry says he commanded the fleet; the article says he was appointed to a commission and that New Amsterdam surrendered to him. The text describes the commission and expedition without calling him the fleet's commander.
The article says Luithold II gave the lordship to Rudolf I of Hachberg-Sausenberg in 1311 and died in 1316; the entry says the castle passed in 1315. The year of the transfer is left out.
The article dates the founding to 1774 and the extension of the monopoly to all of Greenland to 1776; the entry dates the founding to 1776. No founding year is given in the text.
The article gives his birth as the 1290s; the entry has c. 1290. No birth year is given in the text.

The article says the French Académie found it to be Byzantine crystal, later studies an Islamic piece, and also that the hypothesis of plain green glass was first advanced in 1800; the entry says it proved to be glass. The text says only that it was found not to be an emerald.

The article gives his birth as 1 July 1904 in the lead and 7 April 1904 in the biography; the day is left out. The article's lead dates his headship of the government from 1962, its body from his election in 1961; the text follows the entry's 1961.

The article says the town was slowly abandoned from about 1052, when the Taifa of Seville conquered the taifa, and continued to decline in Christian times; the entry says it declined after the Christian conquest of the 13th century. The start of the decline is left out. The article spells the town Salthish, the entry Shaltish; the name is left out of the text.

The article places his authorisation of the Bernays campaign in 1953, after his retirement as president in late 1951; both are given as it has them. The entry dates his leadership of United Fruit from 1933; the article gives no year for his takeover, so none is given.

The article's genealogy from the Bhakti-ratnakara makes Kumara the father of Sanatana, Rupa and Vallabha, while its Birth section makes Mukunda their father; the father is not named in the text. The article spells the first work Brihat-bhagavtamrita; it is not named in the text, as the entry names it.
The article says he served as Grand Duke sometime between 1392 and his death, first recorded in 1404; the sale of Konavle in 1419 named in the entry is not in the article.
The criticisms of the society (school drop-out, coerced initiation, threats against the journalist Mae Azango) are left out for length; the survey figure is given as dated.
The article gives his death as 4 September 1854 or, according to one source, 20 November 1854; only the year is given. José Tomás Boves, named in the entry, is not in the article.
The article treats the dating and the existence of a separate Satakarni II as disputed; the text gives the views it names.
The article dates the culture 700-1200, the entry the 7th to 13th centuries; neither range is given in the text. The entry places it in Hokkaido; the article in northern Honshu and southern Hokkaido.

The article dates his accession to 310 BC and his death to 309 BC; the entry gives 310/309 BCE. No year is given in the text. The entry names Diodorus as the source of the account; the article does not. The article has under 300 words; the text keeps close to all of it.
The article says Hahn established the school with the support of Prince Maximilian; the entry names both as founders. The text does not say who founded it alone.

The article says the title was granted posthumously, in 1760; the entry says he was rewarded with it. The text does not date the grant. The article credits the defence of the city to Blas de Lezo; the entry to Eslava together with Lezo. The text gives Lezo's forces without saying who directed the defence.

The article dates the war 1552-1555; the entry 1552-1554. No end year is given. The article dates the Peace of Passau to August 1553; it is left out. The destruction of Schweinfurt in 1554, named in the entry, is not in the article.

The article says Serfoji ruled first from 1787 to 1793 and again from 1798, Amar Singh usurping the throne in 1793; the entry gives his reign as 1798-1832. The first reign and the year 1793 for Amar Singh's seizure are left out. The article spells the missionary Schwarz; the entry has Schwartz.

The article calls Shah Mir the second Sultan of Kashmir (counting Rinchan); the entry calls him founder of the sultanate. The numbering is left out. The article spells the minister both Bhutta Bhikshana and Bhatta Bhiksana; the second is used.

The article dates his time as dewan 1947 to 1948; the entry says only that he became dewan in 1947, and the end date is left out. The article says the Nawab's constitutional adviser Nabi Baksh recommended joining India; not included to keep the account of Bhutto's own advice as the entry gives it.

The article spells the town Abel-beth-maachah and Abel Beth-Maacah; the entry has Abel-beth-maacah. The article's form is used. The article writes R. Shimon b. Lakish; written out as Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

Two accounts of Nasr's seizure of the citadel exist (before or after Azaz, Ibn al-Adim and Yahya of Antioch); the order is left open in the text. The article calls Thimal Salih's designated successor; not included.

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 200 words of substance, most of it already in the entry (installation in 1700, Shahu's return in 1707, the Kolhapur court, deposition in 1714); it adds only his death of smallpox on 14 March 1726 and the story of an alleged posthumous son, Rajaram II

The article calls the Chūzan Seikan an 18th-century history; the site's entry on Shō Shōken dates its completion to 1650. The century is left out. The article says Hashi succeeded the year after Shishō's death; the succession year is left out.

The article says Shō began compiling the Chūzan Seikan in 1650; the entry says he completed it in 1650. The year is left out. The article gives his life as 1617–1675 and says he died two years after stepping down in 1673; the entry has 1617–1676. The year of death is left out.
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 200 words of substance, nearly all already in the entry. Note: the article has him ascend in 586 BC, the entry's reign starts in 585 BCE

The article calls the projectile probably a large musket ball or grapeshot; the entry says a bullet. The article's own hedged wording is kept and not contradicted. The article does not discuss the dispute over who fired the shot.

The article dates his death and the Battle of Chenggao to 204 BC; the entry has 203 BCE. The year is left out. The article's lead dates Liu Bang's invasion of the Three Qins to 205 BC, its body to 206 BC (as the entry); the year is left out.

The article gives three scholars' dates for his reign (Nilakanta Sastri 555–590, Sailendra Nath Sen 575–600, Mahalingam 575–615) and says hero stones show a reign of at least 33 years; the entry has c. 575–600. The figures are left out.

The article says the city's defences were raised against Tughlaq armies 'who led an army expedition but failed to reach it'; the entry says Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq took the city in 1324. The article's sentence is left out. The article's sentence on Nanyadeva and Vikramaditya VI 'after the reign of Vikramaditya VI in 1076 CE' is garbled; only Lévi's hedged view is kept.
The article's spellings of the Kanva king vary (Susharman, Susarman); both appear as given in their passages. The relief portrait mentioned in the entry is not described in the article.

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 230 words of substance. Note: the article dates his rule c. 1778–1745 BC and has him lead a coalition with Zimri-Lim and Hammurabi against Eshnunna c. 1767 BC before the Elamite War
The article does not mention Benbulben or Nagnata, which the entry names.

The article places the kurgan in central Ukraine; the entry says southern Ukraine. The region is left out. The studied objects (burials, comb, shields, quiver, silver bowl with a hunting scene) come from the titles in the article's literature list, most of them in Russian.

The article gives no account of his death: his fate after the defeat is unknown, so the second section is headed Legacy, not Death and legacy. The entry's statement that Vikramaditya held the southern provinces from Banavasi is not in the article; not repeated.

The article gives the conquest of Tikal as 378 CE and the son's installation as 379, consistent with the entry. The son is called Yax Nuun Ahiin in the article and Yax Nuun Ayiin I in the entry; not named in the text to avoid two spellings on one page.
The article says residential construction fell around 1250 and the mound area was abandoned about 1450, as the entry has it.

The article dates his death to late 1464 or the beginning of 1465; the entry gives d. 1465, so the text gives no year. The article says Božidar is named as his son in some sources and as his brother in others; not used.

The article gives his presidency as 6 December 1860 to 17 April 1862; the entry says he was acting president, so no formal title or dates of office are stated. The article's paragraph headed Retirement and death is about Pretorius's resignation in 1871, not Schoeman; not used.

The article contradicts itself on his death: its lead gives 15 January 1373, its family section 15 January 1372, and its first paragraph 1372; the entry gives d. 1373. No year is given in the text. The article says Gojko and Ivaniš died before 1372; left out because of the dating confusion. The entry's statement that he held lands in the south of Zeta is not in the article; not repeated.
The article gives his death as 13 November 328, consistent with the entry.

The article dates the party's formation as the Sudanese Bloc to 1945 and its affiliation with the RDA to the following year; the entry says it was founded in 1946 as the local section of the RDA. No founding year is given in the text.

The article says Zarmihr Karen helped Kavad regain the throne from Djamasp 'in 488', the year Kavad first came to the throne; this looks like a slip and is left out. The entry gives Zarmihr as another name of Sukhra; the article says he is often confused with his father Zarmihr Hazarwuxt and son Zarmihr Karen. The confusion is left out of the text so as not to contradict the entry's alias; worth checking whether Zarmihr is rightly an alias of Sukhra.

The article names no enemy at Shu’aybah; the entry's British opponent is not contradicted but not named in the text. The article does not describe him as leading the irregulars who set up the Western Thrace government, only as its chief of the general staff.
The article dates the foundation to the 3rd century BC; the entry's 'last centuries BCE' is compatible.

The article dates the effective end of Swedish rule to 1710 and its formal end to the Peace of Nystad of 1721; the text stops at 1710 and leaves 1721 to the entry. The article's scope is all of present-day Estonia, including Swedish Livonia and Ösel; the text concentrates on the Duchy of Estonia.

The entry says Cao Cao's army defeated and killed him; the article specifies capture during the battle and execution afterwards, which does not contradict it. The entry names Yuan Xi among those sheltered; the article names only Yuan Shang.

The article dates the Chola capture to the beginning of the eleventh century and Vishnuvardhana's to about a century later, consistent with the entry's c. 1004 and 1116; no years are repeated. The article's history comes largely from an old gazetteer; its claim that the curse still affects the royal family is left out.

The article gives two population figures (349,000 and 793,000); neither is used. The article's claim that Tama was spoken by an early Yam sub-clan in Egypt is unsupported and left out. The entry's Guéréda hills are not in the article.
The entry's Tuscarora lands, Bath (1705) and the attack of 1711 are not in the article.

The article says some artifacts date to 600 BC and that iron working at Taruga has been firmly dated to 600 BC, the earliest in Sub-Saharan Africa; the entry dates the site to the 4th-3rd century BCE (Fagg's radiocarbon dates) and calls them among the earliest. The 600 BC date and the 'earliest' claim are left out. Left out the 2007 note on calls to protect the site and threats from illegal miners (dated present-day matter). The 1961 trial excavation in the entry is not in the article.

The article gives his dates as 1635-1715 and his reign as 1680-1715, and says the juzes split with his death in 1715; the entry has 'd. c. 1718' and 'after his death around 1718'. The year of his death is left out. The article dates the division into juzes to 1698 while also saying he remained khan of all three; told as the article has it.

The article dates the temple to the 6th century BC without 'late'; the entry's 'late 6th century BCE' is not contradicted. The article says the temple was dedicated to Hera and Apollo; the entry calls it a temple of Hera, which the 1926 votive supports.
The article calls the seven heads naga heads; the entry says cobra heads. Not repeated here.

SKIPPED: The article has about 250 words, most of them already in the entry (date, misnaming as the Temple of Ceres, Doric and Ionic orders); what remains (use as a church around the eighth century, removed in the 1940s) is too little for a longer text.

The article dates the burials and the structure to 150-200 CE; the entry dates the pyramid to about 200-250 CE. No construction date given here. The article gives both 'more than a hundred' and 'two hundred or more' sacrificial burials; the number is left out. The article says the tunnel was believed sealed in 200 CE and 'nearly 1,800 years ago'; left out as it bears on the disputed construction date.
The entry says the Provisions kept the legislators elected on the mainland in office for decades; the article does not say this, so it is not repeated or expanded.

The article dates her deposition to 26 December 1851 (Teurura'i chosen king on 5 January 1852); the entry says she was deposed by Huahine's chiefs in 1852. The date is left out. The article reports an alternative account (Chesneau and Marcantoni) in which another queen, Teuhe I, fought at Maeva; not included. Some sources date the marriage to Pomare II to 8 November 1811 rather than around 1809.
The article calls him prefect of police of the republic; the entry says prefect. Not contradicted.
The article calls the Cross of Theophanu an illuminated manuscript, which seems a slip; the cross is mentioned only by name. The article gives her birth as c. 997; the entry's dates read 997-1058.

The article places the sack by Philip V during the Social War (220-217 BC) without a year; the entry's 218 BCE is not contradicted. The article dates the temple to about 630-610 BC; consistent with the entry's late 7th century BCE.
SKIPPED: The article is mostly lists (places of interest, transport, climate) with under 250 words of substance; its history paragraph and the Mamankam add little beyond the entry.

The entry calls the Tidung largely coastal traders and fishermen; the article describes them as traditionally slash-and-burn farmers, some of them ocean fishermen. The farming is told as the article has it, without denying the trade. Left out the article's remark that their farming methods are often blamed for forest fires (an unattributed present-day accusation).
The entry's date (traditionally 8th century) is not in the article; no date given here.

The article's account is confused in places: it says Munim Khan 'soon died' during the battle but then that loyal soldiers led his horse away and he later signed the treaty; it also has Akbar ordering a flanking attack although he had returned to Fatehpur Sikri. Only the consistent points are used. Dr Abdul Karim's Banglar Itihash, quoted in the article, places Tukaroi in Medinipur district, West Bengal; the entry and the article's lead say Balasore district, Odisha. The alternative is left out.
The article calls the commander Jean-André van der Mersch, the entry Jan Andries van der Mersch; the text uses the surname only.
The article dates the battle to 25 November 1899; the entry says 24 November. The day is left out of the text.
The article names Henry's field marshal in Saxony first as Count Henry of Mansfeld and later as Hoyer of Mansfeld; only the commander killed at Welfesholz, Hoyer, is named in the text.
The article spells the grand prince both Izyaslav and Iziaslav; the entry uses Iziaslav.
Some versions omit Bawo and Magaram and make the seven founders sons of Bayajidda and Daurama; left out as the entry follows the Bawo version.

The article contradicts itself on the locks: four lock complexes built 1910-1912 (two in Serbia, two in Romania) vs a lock system built 1900-1916 with six locks, two in Romania and four in Serbia; left as 'early in the 20th century', no count. Port of Timisoara documented in 1752 vs 'documentary records of the port date back to 1860'; left out.

The entry dates Rhys ap Tewdwr's death to 1093; the article gives 1093 'or perhaps 1094' for the battle in the later accounts, while the chronicle evidence points to 1093. Year left out of the text. Article calls Miles 'High Sheriff of Gloucestershire'; written as sheriff.
Entry's hostage mutilation of 1165 is not in the article; left unmentioned. T. Gwynn Jones's fairy-king etymology left out.

Entry: 'In 1938 ... introduced the Aundh Experiment, a constitution'; article: powers relinquished 1938, Swaraj Constitution adopted January 1939. The constitution's date is left out. Article claims he invented Surya Namaskar; the entry says popularised; 'invented' left out. Article dates Surya Namaskars to 1928 and the Ten-Point Way to Health to 1928 in the list but 1938 for Morgan's edition; kept 1938 for Morgan as the prose gives it.

Entry: occupied from about the 6th century BCE; article: earliest layers c. 800-525 BC. Start date left out of the text. Article says Marshall's excavations ran 1913-1925 in one place and 1913-1934 in another; 1913-1925 used. Article doubts Taxila was ever Achaemenid; entry speaks of the city of the Achaemenid period (a period, not rule), so only the Darius claim and its rebuttal are given.

Article dates the complex's construction 'between the 7th and 12th centuries' and calls the brick Istaliq temple 2nd-3rd century while saying the brick temples were built under the Pandus; only the entry's 11th century stands (not repeated). The 2026 Bhoramdev Corridor plan left out.
The article's account of the court intrigues rests largely on the chronicle Razadarit Ayedawbon.
The article hedges whether he was a local ruler or an Egyptian commander; the entry calls him a ruler and vassal. Both views are given as the scholars' without contradicting the entry.

The article gives the number who left Nova Scotia for Sierra Leone as 1,192, 'nearly 1200' and 'nearly 2,000', and says 4,000 London Black Poor were resettled at Freetown in 1787 as well as that the 1792 migrants 'set up' Freetown; the entry says about 1,100 founded Freetown in 1792. All numbers and the founding left out of the text.
Article gives the confluence as '22 mi (40 km)' west of Birmingham (the conversion is wrong); distance left out. Moundville, named in the entry, is not in the article.
The article dates the ceremony to the night of 14 August 1791 and, in the quoted official history, to 24 August 1791; the entry says August 1791. No day given in the text.
Article gives his birth as c. 1399 (the entry's dates have '?') and his accession as 22 April 1426 (the entry says 1425); both left out of the text.

The article says Saint Malachy founded the abbey in 1161 (he is also said to have arranged the Cistercians' coming from 1142); only his introduction of the order is given. The MacDermots, named in the entry, are not named in the article (only 'the family of the local chieftains').

Article: 'discovered in Asculum (Ascoli), Rome in 1908', an unclear find-place; the entry says found in Rome in 1908. Find-place left out. The article dates the Social War 'around 90 BC'; the entry's 89 BCE grant is not contradicted (no year given in the text).

The article reports a challenge to the received early 10th-century date, arguing that the system was planned in 878-879 under Alfred; the entry says 'probably early tenth century', so the challenge is left out. The article also gives Buckingham's creation as a burh in 918 in one place and its first mention in 914 in another; no year given for it.

Birth given as 1051 and 'possibly 1060' in the article; left out (entry: d. 1111). The article dates the capture of Montgomery Castle 'by 1093' though the revolt broke out in 1094; no year given for it. The 1088 deaths of 'nephews Madog and Rhiryd' left out, as Madog ap Rhiryd kills Cadwgan in 1111.
